rationale: The available literature confirms that heterozygous RAB3A p.Arg83Trp causes spinocerebellar ataxia 52 (SCA52) and that affected individuals exhibit adult-onset cerebellar symptoms frequently accompanied by mild gait spasticity, tremors, and upper motor neuron signs across an ataxia-spasticity spectrum (Miyamoto et al., 2026; Roller et al., 2026; Mouraux et al., 2025). However, the specific quantitative assertion that pyramidal tract signs/mild gait spasticity are present in 'more than 60 percent of adult affected carriers' across Family T and Family K specifically is unsupported by the provided source texts, which describe the sign qualitatively as 'often accompanied by mild gait spasticity' without publishing a verified >60% exact numerator/denominator breakdown in the accessible record.

evidence.text: Miyamoto et al. describe two families with autosomal-dominant cerebellar ataxia harboring heterozygous RAB3A c.247C>T p.(Arg83Trp), reporting that affected individuals presented with adult-onset cerebellar symptoms often accompanied by mild gait spasticity and tremors, with variable neurodevelopmental features, but do not provide a verified quantitative breakdown exceeding 60% in the accessible text.

source.title: An R83W mutation in Rab3A causes autosomal-dominant cerebellar ataxia
source.quote: Affected individuals presented with adult-onset, gradually progressive cerebellar symptoms, often accompanied by mild gait spasticity and tremors. Variable features of neurodevelopmental disorders were also observed.

evidence.text: Roller et al. establish that the recurrent RAB3A hot spot variant R83W causes spasticity and upper motor neuron signs as part of an overlapping ataxia-spasticity spectrum rather than an isolated cerebellar ataxia, supporting incomplete penetrance and clinical variability of pyramidal signs.

source.title: The RAB3A hot spot variant R83W causes spasticity as part of the ataxia-spasticity spectrum
source.quote: While the predominant feature remains cerebellar ataxia, we show upper motor neuron … phenotype within the spasticity-ataxia spectrum.

evidence.text: Mouraux et al. broaden the clinical spectrum of pathogenic RAB3A variants to include hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), identifying a low overall diagnostic frequency (0.81%) in screening cohorts and demonstrating that pyramidal involvement can vary from absent to predominant spastic paraplegia.

conflicts: The hypothesis posits a specific statistical threshold (>60% of adult affected carriers exhibiting mild gait spasticity in Families T and K), but available primary literature only states spasticity is 'often accompanied' or forms a variable continuum with spastic paraplegia, lacking granular individual-level denominator verification in the source text.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact individual-level penetrance and frequency of pyramidal tract signs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, spastic gait) across all genetically confirmed RAB3A p.Arg83Trp carriers in the international registry?
new_directions.rationale: Resolving precise numerators and denominators across all reported kindreds (including Miyamoto, Mouraux, and Roller cohorts) is required to determine whether spasticity meets criteria for a core diagnostic discriminator versus an optional modifier.

new_directions.question_text: Do non-R83W variants in RAB3A (such as p.Ile27Thr) produce prominent spasticity or pure cerebellar ataxia?
new_directions.rationale: OMIM #621535 and MARRVEL list alternative variants such as Ile27Thr; determining whether spasticity is hot-spot specific to switch II domain alterations (p.Arg83Trp) will clarify genotype-phenotype correlations.
